\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{TCSlib.BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.SurfaceRelaxation}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Gaussian gradient length]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianGradientLength}
\statementsource{boolean-ch11-gaussian-invariance}{pdf-8b2c50cf9621-p019-b001}
\label{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianGradientLength}
\leanok
For a natural number $n$, a function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, and
$x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, define the gradient length at $x$ to be $\left(\sum_{i=1}^n
(Df(x)[e_i])^2\right)^{1/2}$, where $e_i$ is the $i$th coordinate vector and $Df(x)$ is
the Fréchet derivative.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Surface-approximating sequence]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.IsSurfaceApproximatingSequence}
\statementsource{boolean-ch11-gaussian-invariance}{pdf-8b2c50cf9621-p019-b001}
\label{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.IsSurfaceApproximatingSequence}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.standardGaussianMeasure}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, and let
$(f_m)_{m\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of functions $f_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$. The
sequence is surface-approximating for $A$ if every $f_m$ is infinitely continuously
differentiable, takes values in $[0,1]$, and each coordinate derivative $x\mapsto
Df_m(x)[e_i]$ is square-integrable with respect to standard Gaussian measure on
$\mathbb{R}^n$; moreover, $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|f_m(x)-\mathbf{1}_A(x)|\,d\gamma_n(x)\to
0$ as $m\to\infty$, where $\gamma_n$ is standard Gaussian measure.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Relaxed Gaussian surface area]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.relaxedGaussianSurfaceArea}
\statementsource{boolean-ch11-gaussian-invariance}{pdf-8b2c50cf9621-p019-b001}
\label{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.relaxedGaussianSurfaceArea}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.IsSurfaceApproximatingSequence, BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianGradientLength, BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.standardGaussianMeasure}
Let $n$ be a natural number and $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. Define the relaxed Gaussian
surface area of $A$ as the infimum, over all surface-approximating sequences $(f_m)$ for
$A$, of $\liminf_{m\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|\nabla f_m(x)|\,d\gamma_n(x)$, where
$\gamma_n$ is standard Gaussian measure and $|\nabla f_m(x)|$ is the Euclidean length of
the gradient.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Gaussian Minkowski content]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianMinkowskiContent}
\statementsource{boolean-ch11-gaussian-invariance}{pdf-8b2c50cf9621-p019-b001}
\label{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianMinkowskiContent}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.standardGaussianMeasure}
Let $n$ be a natural number and $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. The Gaussian Minkowski content
of $A$ is the limit inferior, as $\varepsilon$ tends to zero through positive values, of
$\gamma_n\bigl(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial
A)\leq\varepsilon/2\}\bigr)/\varepsilon$, where $\gamma_n$ is standard Gaussian measure
and distance is Euclidean.
\end{definition}

  {BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.relaxedGaussianSurfaceArea}
  {context}
  {boolean-ch11-gaussian-invariance}
  {pdf-8b2c50cf9621-p019-b001}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $A\subseteq\bbr^n$ be measurable. The relaxed
Gaussian surface area of $A$, defined by taking the infimum over smooth sequences of
functions valued in $[0,1]$ that converge to the indicator of $A$ in Gaussian $L^1$ and
whose coordinate derivatives are Gaussian-square-integrable, of the corresponding limit
inferior of their integrated Gaussian gradient lengths, equals the Gaussian surface area
defined by the limit inferior of the normalized disagreement probability under
infinitesimal Gaussian rotations.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Smooth approximation attaining Gaussian surface area]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.averagedGaussianIndicator_attains_surfaceArea}
\label{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.averagedGaussianIndicator_attains_surfaceArea}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.IsSurfaceApproximatingSequence, BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.averagedGaussianIndicator, BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianGradientLength, BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianSurfaceArea, BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.standardGaussianMeasure}
Let $n\ge0$, let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be measurable, and let $\theta_m\in(0,\pi/2)$
for each $m\in\mathbb N$, with $\theta_m\to0$. Write $u_\theta(x)=\int
1_A(\cos\theta\,x+\sin\theta\,y)\,d\gamma_n(y)$, where $\gamma_n$ is standard Gaussian
measure. The functions $u_{\theta_m}$ take values in $[0,1]$, are infinitely
differentiable, and each coordinate derivative belongs to $L^2(\gamma_n)$; moreover,
they converge to $1_A$ in $L^1(\gamma_n)$. Their Gaussian gradient lengths satisfy
\[
\int \mathrm{grad}_\gamma u_{\theta_m}(x)\,d\gamma_n(x)\longrightarrow P_\gamma(A),
\]
where $\mathrm{grad}_\gamma$ denotes the Euclidean norm of the gradient and
$P_\gamma(A)$ is the Gaussian surface area defined by infinitesimal rotations.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Minkowski content of a finite convex union]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianMinkowskiContent_eq_of_finite_convex_union}
\label{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianMinkowskiContent_eq_of_finite_convex_union}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianMinkowskiContent, BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianSurfaceArea}
Let $n,m\ge0$ and let $C_1,\ldots,C_m$ be closed convex subsets of $\mathbb R^n$, each
with nonempty interior, that are pairwise disjoint. Then the Gaussian Minkowski content
of their union equals the Gaussian surface area of their union.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-energy Gaussian Bobkov inequality]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussian_bobkov_finite_energy}
\label{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussian_bobkov_finite_energy}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.closedGaussianProfile, BooleanAnalysis.GaussianSpace.gaussianGradientLength, BooleanAnalysis.ThresholdFunctions.standardGaussianMeasure}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be infinitely
continuously differentiable, take values in $[0,1]$, and have each coordinate partial
derivative in Gaussian $L^2$. Write $\nabla_G f(x)=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (\partial_i
f(x))^2}$, and let $U$ denote the Gaussian profile that equals the Gaussian density at
the Gaussian quantile for inputs in $(0,1)$ and is zero otherwise. Then
\[
U\!\left(\int f\,d\gamma_n\right)\le \int \sqrt{U(f(x))^2+\nabla_G
f(x)^2}\,d\gamma_n(x),
\]
where $\gamma_n$ is standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^n$.
\end{theorem}
